extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and political thinkers (17th-century England); statesmen, clergy, and students of civil philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical political-philosophical essay arguing which doctrines and practices of the Church (especially the Roman clergy) are errors or pernicious because they usurp civil authority and suppress reason. It identifies specific doctrines, linguistic habits, and institutional privileges that sustain spiritual despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private measure of Good is pernicious
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This private measure of Good, is a Doctrine, not onely Vain, but also Pernicious to the Publique State.' — the view that each man judges good/evil by his own passions rather than by public law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: private conscience-as-measure undermines public laws and public safety; exception noted for monks and friars bound by vow. Anti-pattern: allowing individual passions to supplant civil law leads to disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage is not unchastity
rubrics_metrics.description: Refutation of the claim that 'the work of Marriage is repugnant to Chastity, or Continence,' and thus a moral vice — i.e., the doctrine denying marriage to the clergy is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: clerical continence is a Church constitution for usefulness, not a moral standard making marriage sinful. If marriage were inherently incontinence, all marriage would be vice. Anti-pattern: treating ecclesiastical constitutions as universal moral laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous labeling of all non-popular government as tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Counter to 'From Aristotles Civill Philosophy, they have learned, to call all manner of Common-wealths but the Popular ... Tyranny.' — it is an error to call every monarchy or aristocracy 'tyranny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: historical meanings of terms changed; using pejorative names for disliked governments is rhetorical not analytic. Anti-pattern: equating 'monarch' with 'tyrant' simply because the populace dislikes them; misnaming governments fosters faction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error of saying not men but laws govern
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection of the doctrine that in a well-ordered commonwealth 'not Men should govern, but the Laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: laws require the 'Hands, and Swords of men' to be effective; believing that paper alone governs may encourage rebellion by implying law has power without enforcement. Practical criterion: assess whether laws have enforceable sanction, not merely words on paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil law should not extend to private thoughts and conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To extend the power of the Law ... to the very Thoughts, and Consciences of men, by Examination, and Inquisition of what they Hold ... is against the Law of Nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes legitimate civil inquiries (e.g., when appointing a teacher) from coercing private belief. Anti-pattern: punishing individuals for private opinions when their actions are lawful; forcing self-accusation under threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private interpretation of law is an error without commonwealth authority
rubrics_metrics.description: 'For a Private man, without the Authority of the Common-wealth ... to Interpret the Law by his own Spirit, is another Error in the Politiques.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: only the lawgiver (or its authorized interpreters) legitimately explains laws; scriptures function as law only when constituted by the commonwealth. But if the state allows preaching/teaching, others cannot lawfully forbid it. Practical test: does an interpreter have civil authorization?

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscure scholastic language hides truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that 'the Writings of Schoole-Divines, are nothing else ... but insignificant Traines of strange and barbarous words' which render doctrine unintelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: clear, translatable language indicates intelligibility; inability to render a scholastic text into modern tongues shows it is not truly intelligible. Anti-pattern: using obscure jargon to conceal weakness or to shut down inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject relying on tradition, legends, and unverified testimonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning against 'errors brought in from false, or uncertain History' such as legends of miracles, apparitions, and 'the unwritten Word of God' which amount to 'old Wives Fables.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: treat patristic testimony and traditions critically; accept reports only after examination by competent judgment. Anti-pattern: using isolated fathers' reports or popular legend as decisive proof of doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to suppression of true philosophy by ecclesiastical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: 'With the Introduction of False, we may joyn also the suppression of True Philosophy, by such men, as neither by lawfull authority, nor sufficient study, are competent Judges of the truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: true opinions ought to be examined by competent judges; punishment of disputants is only justifiable under civil law when teaching tends to sedition or disobedience. Anti-pattern: ecclesiastical censorship that prevents scientific or natural inquiry without civil cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Cui bono' (who benefits) to infer authorship or motive
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He That Receiveth Benefit By A Fact, Is Presumed To Be The Author' — the rule of presumption of motive from benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: trace which parties obtain profit, honor, or contentment from a doctrine or institution to infer who likely produced or sustained it. Example: doctrines that establish spiritual sovereignty benefit clergy and so are suspect as engineered for power.

rubrics_metrics.name: The doctrine that the Church militant is the present kingdom of God serves worldly power
rubrics_metrics.description: Position: teaching that 'The Present Church Now Militant On Earth, Is The Kingdome Of God' has been used to claim pastoral/rightful governing power over commonwealths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: accepting this doctrine supplies a warrant for clerical governance, usurping civil sovereignty. Anti-pattern: conflating spiritual office with civil rulership; evaluate doctrines by their political effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal infallibility secures obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That the Pope In His Publique Capacity Cannot Erre' — doctrine of papal infallibility creates readiness to obey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: claiming infallibility functions politically to centralize obedience. Evaluative test: whether a doctrinal claim concentrates authority and diminishes civil checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine that bishops receive authority from the pope (rather than God or sovereign) creates foreign dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'All other Bishops ... have not their Right ... but from the Pope' — this doctrine makes bishops dependent on a foreign prince and destabilizes civil sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political consequence: episcopal subordination to a foreign power provides a channel for raising civil unrest and interference. Anti-pattern: ecclesiastical chains of authority that bypass the civil sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions of the clergy from civil law are harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The exemption of these, and of all other Priests ... from the Power of the Civill Laws' creates a privileged class not liable for public burdens or penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: exempted clergy avoid taxation, punishments, and civic duties; they owe allegiance primarily to the pope rather than the state. Criterion: institutions should not create large segments of society immune to civil law enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using sacerdotal titles and calling the Lord's Supper a sacrifice transfers civil prerogatives to clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Giving to their Priests ... the name of Sacerdotes, that is, Sacrificers ... the making the Lords Supper a Sacrifice' gives the clergy the aura and authority of ancient public ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: names and liturgical categorizations confer perceived continuity with Old-Testament public power; evaluate whether liturgical terminology functions to justify secular authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Matrimony a sacrament gives clergy judicial power over legitimacy and succession
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Sacramentation Of Marriage ... giveth to the Clergy the Judging of the lawfulnesse of Marriages' — doctrinal framing that grants clerical jurisdiction over succession and inheritances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political impact: control over marriage affects hereditary rights and monarchy succession; assess doctrines for effects on civil inheritance rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denying marriage to priests secures succession-control
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Deniall of Marriage to Priests, serveth to assure this Power of the pope over Kings' — clerical celibacy used to prevent dynastic claims independent of papal influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: preventing priests (or potential monarchs made clerics) from producing heirs ties temporal power to ecclesiastical favor. Anti-pattern: institutional rules that limit civic continuity to increase dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auricular confession as intelligence-gathering and control
rubrics_metrics.description: 'From Auricular Confession, they obtain ... better intelligence of the designs of Princes' — private confession supplies clerical knowledge and leverage over political actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political concern: secretive religious practices can be instruments for surveillance and manipulation of state affairs. Criterion: evaluate religious practices for their potential to concentrate confidential political intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonization and declaring martyrs as political tools
rubrics_metrics.description: 'By the Canonization of Saints, and declaring who are Martyrs, they assure their Power' — using sanctification to induce obstinacy against civil laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effect: canonization can mobilize popular resistance to civil authority by sacralizing opposition. Anti-pattern: religious exaltation used to legitimize civil disobedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of priestly power over transubstantiation, penance, and absolution secure spiritual authority
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They assure the same, by the Power they ascribe to every Priest, of making Christ; and by the Power of ordaining Pennance; and of Remitting, and Retaining of sins.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: sacramental and juridical powers over salvation create dependence on clergy. Evaluation: doctrines that make clergy gatekeepers of salvation centralize spiritual and thus temporal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrines of purgatory, indulgences and external works enrich clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: 'By the Doctrine of Purgatory, of Justification by externall works, and of Indulgences, the Clergy is enriched.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: assess economic incentives created by doctrines (e.g., sale of indulgences) and whether they corrupt spiritual aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daemonology and exorcism as fear-based control
rubrics_metrics.description: 'By their Daemonology, and the use of Exorcisme ... they keep (or thinke they keep) the People more in awe of their Power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation: supernatural threat-framing can be used to intimidate and control populations; distinguish genuine pastoral care from manipulation by fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: School-divinity (Aristotelian metaphysics et al.) sustains errors through obscurity and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Metaphysiques, Ethiques, and Politiques of Aristotle, the frivolous Distinctions ... taught in the Universities ... serve them to keep these Errors from being detected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: institutionalized curricula using obscure distinctions can function politically to maintain clerical dominance. Antidote: promote clarity, natural philosophy, and moral reasoning accessible to the laity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power is preserved by the virtues by which it was acquired, not by suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Power is preserved by the same Vertues by which it is acquired; that is to say, by Wisdome, Humility, Clearnesse of Doctrine, and sincerity of Conversation; and not by suppression ... nor by obscure Language ... nor by Pious Frauds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive norm for legitimate pastors: retain authority through genuine virtue and clear doctrine, not by deception or oppression. Evaluation metric: measure clergy legitimacy by exhibited virtues rather than coercive practices.
